nameStory: The 'salted' part of this lichen's name comes from its distinctive white, powdery coating that looks like someone sprinkled salt over its surface. The 'starburst' refers to its radiating, leaf-like lobes that spread outward from the center like a firework frozen in time.
description: Salted Starburst Lichen is a leafy (foliose) lichen that forms flat, spreading patches on tree bark. Its gray-green lobes radiate outward in a star-like pattern, covered with a distinctive white, powdery coating called soredia. These patches typically grow 2-4 inches across, creating circular to irregular colonies that can merge together on favorable bark surfaces.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: The upper surface has a distinctive white, powdery coating that feels slightly chalky to the touch - this is the lichen's way of reproducing without forming fruiting bodies

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms flat, leafy patches with lobes that radiate outward from the center like spokes of a wheel, creating a starburst appearance

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Gray-green to pale greenish-gray when dry, becoming more vibrant green when wet, always with the characteristic white powdery coating on top

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost always found on the bark of deciduous trees, particularly favoring smooth-barked species like maple, ash, and cherry

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual colonies typically 2-4 inches across, but multiple colonies often grow together to form larger patches several feet wide

habitat: Look for Salted Starburst Lichen on the bark of deciduous trees in mature forests throughout New England, from sea level to moderate elevations. It particularly favors trees with relatively smooth bark like maples, ashes, and cherry trees in areas with good air quality. You'll often find it in mixed hardwood forests and along forest edges where there's partial shade and good air circulation.

seasonality.spring: The white powdery coating becomes more noticeable as humidity increases, and the lichen appears more vibrant green when wet from spring rains.
seasonality.summer: During dry periods, the lichen appears more gray and the white powdery coating is most prominent. Look for it on the shaded sides of trees.
seasonality.fall: Autumn moisture makes the green color more pronounced, and the contrast with the white coating is particularly striking against colorful fall foliage.
seasonality.winter: The white powdery surface stands out beautifully against dark wet bark and snow, making this actually one of the easier seasons to spot this species.

funFact: The white powder covering this lichen contains tiny reproductive packages called soredia - each speck is like a microscopic care package containing both the fungus and algae needed to start a new lichen colony, ready to blow away in the wind to colonize new trees.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with its close relative American Starburst Lichen, but Salted Starburst always has that distinctive white powdery coating while American Starburst lacks this feature and instead produces small finger-like projections called isidia.
compareHints: The key difference from its cousin American Starburst Lichen is the reproductive strategy - Salted Starburst reproduces with white powdery soredia while American Starburst uses small coral-like projections called isidia. Both have the same radiating growth pattern, but only Salted Starburst looks like it's been dusted with flour or salt.

relatedSpecies.distinction: American Starburst Lichen differs from its close relative, Salted Starburst Lichen, primarily in its range and subtle chemical differences that require laboratory testing to distinguish.
